incidents.title: Liveness equals readiness
incidents.brief: A pod is killed because /health fails while the process is only warming a cache.
incidents.constraint: The process is alive but not ready for traffic.
incidents.question: How should probes be split?

choices.label: Split probes
choices.resultBody: Liveness means the process should be restarted; readiness means it can receive traffic.

choices.label: Kill on warmup
choices.resultBody: Every restart throws away the half-built cache, so the pod never finishes warming and errors stay at 120 while the pool shrinks.

choices.label: No readiness
choices.resultBody: Without a readiness gate the balancer sends requests to the warming pod immediately; its cache misses push p95 past 200 ms and errors climb.

hints: The balancer still thinks this node is fine.
Alive is not the same as ready.
Probe the serving path.

incidents.title: Health probes pin the orders primary at 92% CPU
incidents.brief: Grocerly's 400 pods answer readiness every 2 s from kubelet and 3 load balancers by running SELECT count(*) FROM orders. That's 800 full-index scans a second; primary CPU sits at 92%.
incidents.constraint: A pod that has lost its database connection must still leave rotation within 30 s.
incidents.question: How can readiness reflect database health without loading it?

choices.label: Serve readiness from pool status refreshed by SELECT 1 every 10 s

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Readiness may be up to 10 s stale; DB load from probes drops ~99%.

choices.resultBody: Each pod runs one cheap SELECT 1 on an existing pool connection every 10 s and caches the result; probes read that flag in microseconds. Probe load on the primary falls from 800 scans to 40 trivial queries a second, and a pod with a dead pool still goes unready within 30 s. Cost: readiness can be up to 10 s stale.

choices.label: Point the health query at a read replica instead
choices.resultBody: The replica now burns 90% CPU on count(*) and its replication lag climbs, while readiness reports the replica's health instead of the primary's, so pods that lost the primary stay in rotation.

choices.label: Lower the probe frequency from every 2 s to every 30 s
choices.resultBody: Scans drop 15x and CPU recovers, but with a failure threshold of 3 a dead pod now takes 90 s to leave rotation, which breaks the 30 s requirement, and every probe is still a full index scan.

hints: Multiply pods by probers by frequency and look at what each probe does.
A health check should cost almost nothing to answer.
Separate how often you learn about the database from how often you're asked.

incidents.title: Full-disk pod stays in rotation, failing every upload
incidents.brief: One of Snapdocs' 12 upload pods filled its local scratch disk. Every upload there fails with ENOSPC, yet /health returns a static 200, so the balancer keeps sending it 8% of 3,000 uploads/s.
incidents.constraint: Readiness must not depend on shared services, which would pull every pod at once.
incidents.question: What should this pod's readiness actually check?

choices.label: Fail readiness when the pod's scratch disk drops below 5% free

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Readiness checks local prerequisites only; still fix cleanup so pods don't fill.

choices.resultBody: Readiness now checks what this pod's request path needs locally: free scratch space, config loaded, listener up. pod-7 turns unready within one probe period and stops receiving uploads while an alert fires to fix the leak. Because it checks only local state, no shared outage can empty the pool. Cost: you still need to fix disk cleanup.

choices.label: Make /health write and read a row in shared Postgres
choices.resultBody: The row lands on Postgres's disk, not pod-7's, so the probe stays green and failures continue, and a Postgres blip would now mark all 12 pods unready at once.

choices.label: Alert on-call when any pod's disk passes 90% usage
choices.resultTitle: Someone gets paged, uploads keep failing
choices.resultBody: Visibility improves, but a human takes about 25 minutes to acknowledge and cordon the pod, and during that time it keeps failing 8% of uploads at full rate.

hints: The endpoint says 'the process is running', which was never the question.
What does this pod need locally to serve a request successfully?
Readiness should fail on local conditions that break this pod's request path.

incidents.title: Vendor blip empties the whole pool
incidents.brief: ShopRail's readiness probe calls the payment vendor. A 40-second vendor blip marked all 60 pods unready at once, so the balancer returned 503 for catalog pages too, at 30k req/s.
incidents.constraint: Catalog and search must keep serving even when payments are down.
incidents.question: What should the readiness probe actually check?

choices.label: Readiness checks local state; vendor call behind a circuit breaker
choices.resultBody: Pods stay ready while the vendor is down; the breaker fails checkout fast with a "try again shortly" page. 503s drop from 30,000/s to ~450/s (checkout only). Cost: vendor health now needs its own alert.

choices.label: Raise readiness failureThreshold from 3 to 10 probes
choices.resultBody: The pool now drains 100 s into an outage instead of 30 s. This 40 s blip would pass, but the next 3-minute vendor outage still takes all 60 pods out and 28,500 catalog req/s fail.

choices.label: Cache the vendor health result in each pod for 60 s
choices.resultBody: All 60 pods cache the same vendor answer, so they expire and flip within the same minute. During a 3-minute outage ready pods still hit 4 of 60 and catalog 503s return.

hints: Every pod failed for the same external reason at the same moment.
Readiness should answer "can this pod serve?", not "is every vendor healthy?".
Keep shared dependencies out of per-pod probes and degrade the one feature that needs them.

incidents.title: JVM pods restart forever during boot
incidents.brief: LedgerCore's JVM needs 90 s to load 2 GB of reference data, but liveness kills it at 30 s. All 24 new pods crash-loop and the deploy is stuck at 0 ready.
incidents.constraint: Once running, a hung pod must still be restarted within 30 seconds.
incidents.question: Which probe setup survives a 90-second boot?

choices.label: startupProbe with a 120 s budget, then 30 s liveness
choices.resultBody: Liveness is suspended until the startup probe passes (every 10 s, up to 12 failures), so pods finish their 90 s boot and all 24 go ready; a hung pod is still killed in 30 s. Cost: a pod stuck during boot lingers up to 120 s.

choices.label: Stretch the liveness failure window to 120 seconds
choices.resultTitle: Boot works, hangs now last 2 minutes
choices.resultBody: The crash loop ends, but the 120 s window applies forever. The next deadlocked pod served 500s for two minutes before anything restarted it, breaking the 30-second rule.

choices.label: Drop liveness and let readiness gate slow pods
choices.resultBody: Pods boot, but a pod that deadlocks now just goes unready and stays that way. By morning 6 of 24 pods were stuck, cutting capacity 25% with nothing restarting them.

hints: The process is not broken; it is still booting when it gets killed.
Boot needs a long timeout and steady state needs a short one.
Kubernetes has a separate probe that holds off liveness until the first success.

incidents.title: Botnet floods the public /health endpoint
incidents.brief: Parcelio's /health is reachable at api.parcelio.com/health and runs a deep check of 5 dependencies. A botnet is sending 25k req/s to it, and it also leaks version numbers and internal hostnames.
incidents.constraint: The cloud load balancer's health checks cannot send custom headers.
incidents.question: How do you keep probes working without exposing them?

choices.label: Serve probes on an internal port the public ingress never routes

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Second listener and security-group rule; public 404s /health.

choices.resultTitle: Bots hit a 404 at the edge
choices.resultBody: Probes move to :8081, reachable only from the load balancer's and kubelet's subnets, and ingress returns 404 for /health. The flood dies at the edge, the deep dependency check no longer runs on attacker demand, and version details stop leaking. Cost: a second listener and one firewall rule.

choices.label: Rate-limit /health to 100 requests per second per IP
choices.resultBody: The botnet spans 40k IPs sending a few requests each, far under the limit, so most of the flood still runs deep checks; meanwhile the load balancer's own probes come from a handful of IPs and start getting 429s.

choices.label: Require an API key header on /health requests
choices.resultTitle: The balancer can't send the key
choices.resultBody: Bots are rejected, but so is the load balancer, which cannot add custom headers to its checks; every target is marked unhealthy and the whole API goes dark.

hints: Only two kinds of callers ever need this endpoint.
Filtering by who is asking fails when the legitimate caller can't identify itself.
Make the endpoint unreachable from the internet rather than trying to filter it.

incidents.title: Sidecar keeps dead app containers in rotation
incidents.brief: Meshly's pods run the app plus an Envoy sidecar. Readiness probes Envoy's admin /ready, which returns 200 whenever Envoy is up. When the app container crashes, the pod stays ready and 6% of requests 503.
incidents.constraint: The service mesh sidecar must stay in every pod.
incidents.question: What should the readiness probe be asking?

choices.label: Probe the app container's own readiness endpoint and port

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Probe config per container; sidecar still needs its own liveness.

choices.resultBody: Readiness now targets the app's own /ready on its port, so when the app process dies the probe fails and the pod leaves the Service endpoints within 10 s, even though Envoy is still healthy. Envoy keeps its own liveness check. Cost: probe config has to stay in sync with the app's port.

choices.label: Probe Envoy's admin endpoint every second instead of 10
choices.resultTitle: Faster probes of the wrong thing
choices.resultBody: Envoy is perfectly healthy, so probing it ten times as often just returns 200 ten times as often; the crashed app containers stay in rotation and 503s don't move.

choices.label: Switch to a TCP probe on Envoy's inbound listener
choices.resultTitle: The listener accepts, the app is gone
choices.resultBody: Envoy's listener accepts TCP connections whether or not the app behind it is alive, so the handshake succeeds, the probe passes, and requests still get 503 from the missing upstream.

hints: The probe got a correct answer to the wrong question.
In a pod with two containers, which one actually serves the request?
Health must be measured at the component that does the work.

incidents.title: Pods flap in and out every 10 s
incidents.brief: Streamly's readiness probe has a 1 s timeout on a dependency whose p99 is 1.2 s. 40% of 80 pods flip unready every other probe, and the balancer sprays 502s at 45k req/s.
incidents.constraint: Genuinely broken pods must still leave rotation within 30 seconds.
incidents.question: How do you stop the flapping without hiding real failures?

choices.label: Hysteresis: eject after 3 failed probes, re-admit after 2
choices.resultTitle: One slow probe no longer ejects
choices.resultBody: A single 1.2 s probe no longer ejects a pod; three misses in a row (30 s) do, and two passes re-admit it. Rotation changes fall from 190/min to 3 and 502s from 2,600/s to 40. Cost: a dead pod can linger 30 s, so LB retries must cover it.

choices.label: Probe every 1 second so recovery is detected faster
choices.resultBody: Ten times more probes means ten times more chances to hit the 1.2 s tail. Rotation changes jump to 1,100/min, probe traffic adds 8 points of CPU, and 502s rise to 3,400/s.

choices.label: Remove the readiness probe and rely on LB passive retries
choices.resultBody: Flapping stops, but new and crashed pods now get traffic until the balancer sees real errors. Each rollout sprays about 1,500 502s/s for 20 seconds.

hints: The pods are not failing; the probe is measuring a 1.2 s tail with a 1 s ruler.
A single sample should not flip a binary decision back and forth.
Use different thresholds for leaving and rejoining rotation.

incidents.title: Exec probes eat 40% of each pod's CPU
incidents.brief: Quillr's liveness and readiness are exec probes running 'python healthcheck.py' every 2 s. Each run boots an interpreter for 180 ms of CPU; on 500m-limited pods that's 40% of CPU and heavy throttling.
incidents.constraint: The CPU limit stays at 500m per pod.
incidents.question: How do you check the app without paying for a new process each time?

choices.label: Replace exec probes with httpGet to an in-process endpoint

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: App must expose a lightweight handler; no new process per probe.

choices.resultBody: The kubelet sends an HTTP GET to a handler inside the already-running process, which answers from in-memory state in well under a millisecond. No fork, no interpreter start-up, so the 180 ms of CPU per probe disappears and throttling falls from 62% to 3%. Cost: the app must expose a small handler.

choices.label: Raise each pod's CPU limit from 500m to 2 cores
choices.resultBody: Latency recovers, but requests plus limits now reserve 4x the CPU, the cluster needs 60 more nodes, and the probes still waste the same 180 ms each; the constraint says the limit can't move.

choices.label: Raise the probe timeoutSeconds from 1 to 10
choices.resultBody: Slow throttled probes stop timing out, so there are fewer spurious restarts, but every probe still forks a Python interpreter every 2 s, so CPU stays pegged and p99 latency doesn't improve.

hints: Look at what it costs to run the probe, not what it checks.
Starting a process is far more expensive than answering a request.
Let the running app answer the probe itself.

incidents.title: Every rolling deploy spikes 502s for 30 seconds
incidents.brief: Tripwise deploys 30 times a day. On SIGTERM its Go server exits immediately, but the load balancer keeps routing to the pod for another 5-10 s. Each deploy drops 3% of 50k req/s.
incidents.constraint: Deploys must stay rolling and happen many times a day.
incidents.question: How does a terminating pod leave without dropping requests?

choices.label: preStop sleep 15 s, then stop accepting and finish in-flight requests

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Each pod takes ~25 s longer to terminate; deploys take a few minutes longer.

choices.resultTitle: The balancer lets go before the pod does
choices.resultBody: The preStop hook sleeps 15 s while endpoint removal propagates to the balancer, so new requests stop arriving; then SIGTERM triggers http.Server.Shutdown, which finishes in-flight requests within the 30 s grace period. Deploy 502s fall to near zero. Cost: every pod takes about 25 s longer to terminate.

choices.label: Raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds from 30 to 300
choices.resultBody: The grace period is only the maximum time Kubernetes waits before SIGKILL; the app still exits the instant it gets SIGTERM, so the 5-10 s window of misrouted requests is unchanged.

choices.label: Retry every 502 at the API gateway once
choices.resultBody: Most reads succeed on retry, but a 502 doesn't tell you whether a POST reached the app, so some bookings are now created twice while others still fail when the retry lands on another terminating pod.

hints: Removing a pod from the load balancer is not instant.
The pod and the balancer need to agree on who stops first.
Keep serving briefly after you're told to stop, then drain what's in flight.

incidents.title: Green probe, one pod failing 38%
incidents.brief: One of 12 Ridely dispatch pods has a corrupted local model file. /healthz returns 200, but 38% of that pod's requests 500, about 600 errors/s at 20k req/s.
incidents.constraint: The probe must stay cheap; it cannot replay a full dispatch request every 5 seconds.
incidents.question: What removes a pod that passes probes but fails real traffic?

choices.label: Passive outlier ejection after 5 consecutive real 5xx responses
choices.resultTitle: Real traffic ejects the bad pod
choices.resultBody: The mesh sees pod-7's run of 5xx on live requests and ejects it within about 2 s for a 30 s back-off; 5xx fall from 600/s to 5/s. Cost: cap ejection at 10% of the pool, or a fleet-wide bug would eject everyone.

choices.label: Make /healthz replay a full synthetic dispatch request
choices.resultTitle: Probes now eat 18 points of CPU
choices.resultBody: Each probe runs a 150 ms dispatch on all 12 pods every 5 s. It catches pod-7 eventually, but under load the heavy probe times out and starts ejecting healthy pods too.

choices.label: Retry each failed dispatch once on a different pod
choices.resultBody: Most failures succeed on retry, but pod-7 stays in rotation, each failure costs a second request, and p95 climbs from 180 to 320 ms while the corrupted model is never removed.

hints: The probe and the real request take different code paths.
You already have thousands of real requests per second telling you which pod is bad.
Let the proxy judge each backend by its observed error streak.

incidents.title: Payments RPCs fail on pods reporting SERVING
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's binary serves Ledger and Payments gRPC services on :9090. On 2 of 8 pods, Payments failed to connect to its HSM at boot, but the probe checks the overall server status, so 25% of Payments RPCs return UNAVAILABLE.
incidents.constraint: Both services must keep running in the same binary for now.
incidents.question: How do you make the probe see the broken service?

choices.label: gRPC readiness probe naming the payments.v1.Payments service

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Pods with broken Payments also stop serving Ledger until they recover or are split out.

choices.resultTitle: The probe asks about Payments by name
choices.resultBody: The gRPC health protocol reports status per service name; the probe now sends service 'payments.v1.Payments', gets NOT_SERVING from the 2 broken pods and pulls them from endpoints. Payments errors fall to near zero. Cost: those pods stop serving Ledger too, a reason to split the services later.

choices.label: Use a TCP socket probe on port 9090
choices.resultBody: The gRPC server is listening, so the TCP handshake succeeds on all 8 pods; a socket probe knows nothing about which services inside are able to work, and 25% of Payments RPCs still fail.

choices.label: Probe the HTTP metrics endpoint on port 8080 instead
choices.resultBody: The Prometheus handler runs on its own listener and happily returns 200 while Payments is NOT_SERVING, so the two broken pods stay in rotation.

hints: The process is healthy; one of the things it serves is not.
The gRPC health protocol can answer about more than the whole server.
Ask about the specific service your callers depend on.

incidents.title: Recovered pods collapse again when readmitted together
incidents.brief: After a cache outage, all 200 of Menuly's pods turned ready within 5 s and got full traffic with cold local caches. Database QPS jumped 12x, pods timed out, went unready and the cycle repeated for 40 minutes.
incidents.constraint: The database can take at most 3x its normal query rate.
incidents.question: How should recovered pods re-enter rotation?

choices.label: Enable load-balancer slow start to ramp new targets over 90 s

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Full capacity returns ~90 s later; the database sees a gentle ramp instead of a spike.

choices.resultTitle: Caches warm on a gentle ramp
choices.resultBody: Newly healthy targets start at a small share of traffic and ramp linearly over 90 s, so local caches fill while load is low and database QPS peaks at about 2.5x instead of 12x. Pods stay ready and the flapping loop never starts. Cost: full capacity returns about 90 s later after an outage.

choices.label: Add a 60-second initialDelaySeconds to the readiness probe
choices.resultBody: The delay only affects container start, and here pods were already running; even where it applies, all 200 pods still become ready in the same second after 60 s, with caches just as cold.

choices.label: Scale from 200 to 400 pods to spread the load
choices.resultBody: Each new pod starts with an empty cache too, so twice as many pods send cache-miss queries at once and database QPS climbs further; the database, not the pods, is the bottleneck.

hints: The pods were right to say they were ready, yet they still couldn't take full load.
Warm-up state like caches is invisible to a readiness check.
Control how quickly traffic returns, not just whether it returns.

incidents.title: Busy pods fail probes and get pulled under load
incidents.brief: During a flash sale, BuyNow's traffic doubled to 90k req/s. Readiness requests queued behind 800 requests in each pod's worker pool, timed out at 1 s, and 40% of pods were ejected, overloading the rest.
incidents.constraint: Truly dead pods must still leave rotation within 15 s.
incidents.question: How do you stop load from looking like failure?

choices.label: Answer probes on a dedicated thread; shed excess load with 429

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Some users see 429 at peak; the fleet keeps its full capacity.

choices.resultTitle: Busy pods stay in and say 'slow down'
choices.resultBody: The probe handler runs on its own small listener outside the request queue, so an overloaded pod still answers in milliseconds, while an admission limit returns 429 for the 8% of requests beyond capacity. The fleet keeps all its pods, and dead ones still fail within 15 s. Cost: some shoppers see 'try again' at peak.

choices.label: Raise readiness timeoutSeconds from 1 to 10
choices.resultBody: Fewer probes time out, but at peak the queue delay exceeds 10 s too, so 15% of pods still get pulled, and a genuinely hung pod now takes 30 s to leave rotation, breaking the 15 s rule.

choices.label: Autoscale on probe failures to add pods faster
choices.resultBody: New pods need 90 s to schedule and boot, while ejections cascade in seconds; by the time they arrive the remaining pods have also failed probes, and each new pod is ejected as soon as it fills up.

hints: The ejected pods were working hard, not broken.
When a probe waits in the same queue as real traffic, it measures queue length.
Keep health answers independent of request load, and handle overload separately.

incidents.title: Deadlocked pod passes liveness for 6 hours
incidents.brief: One of Routely's 20 JVM pods deadlocked: all 200 worker threads wait on two locks. Liveness is served by a separate Netty thread that returns 200, so 5% of requests hang for 30 s until someone notices.
incidents.constraint: Liveness must not restart pods that are merely busy.
incidents.question: How can liveness detect that no work is making progress?

choices.label: Liveness fails if no worker finished a task in 60 s while work is queued

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Needs a heartbeat counter in the worker loop; slow-but-moving pods are left alone.

choices.resultBody: Each worker bumps a completed-task counter; liveness fails when the queue is non-empty and the counter hasn't moved for 60 s. A deadlocked pod is restarted within about 90 s, while a busy pod that is still completing tasks passes. Also capture a thread dump before restart to fix the lock order. Cost: a small watchdog in the worker loop.

choices.label: Serve the liveness endpoint from the worker thread pool
choices.resultBody: The deadlocked pod now fails liveness, but so does every pod whose pool is saturated at peak; the kubelet restarts busy pods, the survivors get more load, and a restart storm follows.

choices.label: Restart every pod on a nightly schedule
choices.resultBody: A deadlock that starts at 9 a.m. still hangs 5% of requests for 15 hours until the scheduled restart, and the root cause is never captured.

hints: The thread answering the probe was fine; the threads doing the work were not.
'Busy' and 'stuck' look the same from a queue, but not from a completion counter.
Liveness should measure forward progress, not whether something can answer HTTP.

incidents.title: Redis failover restarts every pod
incidents.brief: Bookly's liveness probe pings Redis. A 25-second Redis primary failover failed liveness on all 48 pods; Kubernetes restarted them together and cold JVMs took 4 minutes to serve 18k req/s again.
incidents.constraint: Redis is only a cache; the app can serve from Postgres, more slowly, while Redis is away.
incidents.question: What should the liveness probe depend on?

choices.label: Liveness checks only the process; Redis loss degrades to Postgres
choices.resultTitle: Pods ride out the Redis failover
choices.resultBody: Next Redis failover, pods stay alive and read through to Postgres; p95 rises to about 140 ms for 25 s instead of a 4-minute outage. Cost: Postgres takes ~3x reads in that window, so its connection pool must be capped.

choices.label: Raise the liveness timeout so Redis failover finishes first
choices.resultBody: This failover would pass, but next week's 60-second failover still restarted all 48 pods at once, and genuinely hung pods now take 40 s longer to be caught.

choices.label: Move the Redis ping from liveness into readiness
choices.resultBody: Nothing restarts now, but all 48 pods go unready together while Redis fails over. The balancer has no targets and returns 18,000 503s/s for 25 s even though Postgres could have served.

hints: Restarting a pod cannot fix Redis, but it can throw away warm JVMs.
A shared dependency in any per-pod probe fails every pod at once.
Ask whether this pod would be healthier after a restart; if not, the check does not belong in liveness.
